info.bio:
Moulty perdio la mano en un accidente, pero eso no le iba a impedir tocar la bateria en una banda de rock.
En 1963, forma The Barbarians junto a tres muchachos ansiosos.
Pelos largos, sandalias, caras de bobos y garfios, ese era el look de estos forajidos.
En este disco The Barbarians - Are You A Boy Or Are You A Girl? (1966)
podremos escuchar covers de la talla de "..Rising Sun", "Susie Q", "Bo Diddley" y otros.
Tocaban un ritmo beat con clara (demasiada) influencia de Dylan.

books.title: 1966: The Year the Decade Exploded (Jon Savage)

scenes.name: Los rockers de garaje
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: En 1966 no tenían nombre (Billboard los llamaba «rockers»); hoy se les llama grupos de garaje. La respuesta creativa americana a la invasión británica: chicos blancos de suburbio que ensayaban en el garaje familiar y tocaban en gimnasios, iglesias y fiestas, con cortes de pelo de Brian Jones, actitud de Jagger, fuzz, rave-ups a lo Yardbirds, Them y Stones y, casi siempre, un órgano Farfisa o Vox con un regusto siniestro de película de terror de autocine. Recuperaban la línea del rock americano de 1963-1964 (Kingsmen, Trashmen) que los Beatles cortaron en seco: «Hanky Panky» de Tommy James, grabado en 1963, fue número 1 en julio de 1966. Ese septiembre las listas se llenaron de discos duros: «96 Tears» de ? and the Mysterians (mexicanoamericanos de Flint, con un órgano hipnótico de otro disco), «Dirty Water» de los Standells, «You’re Gonna Miss Me» de los 13th Floor Elevators y «Psychotic Reaction» de Count Five, calco del «I’m a Man» de los Yardbirds. Quejas dirigidas a las mujeres, pero también una nueva confianza; quejas pequeñas que empezaban a encontrar un objetivo, como en «One of These Days» de los Roosters.

podcast.title: Mid-60s Garage Band
podcast.body: The Barbarians were part of a series of rough, ragged, and raw-sounding bands in the 1960s that came from North American garages and basements. Their attire, which often included leather jackets, contributed to a rebellious image likened to Marlon Brando or James Dean, causing some to describe these musicians as looking like "punks." "There was the count five, the barbarians, the standels, the trogs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Original Garage Rock Band with Punk Style
podcast.body: The Barbarians were an original Garage Rock band from Massachusetts. They embraced an early "punk" aesthetic by dressing in black leather jackets, reminiscent of the motorcycle gang punk portrayed by Marlon Brando in the 1953 film "The Wild Ones." Their drummer, Dermammolton, notably played with a hook in place of his missing left hand. "Some of these bands, like the barbarians, who were from Massachusetts, dressed in black leather jackets, reminiscent of the motorcycle gang punk portrayed by Marlon Brando in movies like The Wild Ones from 1953."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rock Revivals Part 4: Garage Rock

xref.title: Mid-60s Garage Band
xref.body: The Standells were among the rough, ragged, and raw-sounding bands of the 1960s originating from garages and basements across North America. Their adoption of tough imagery, frequently involving leather jackets, prompted observers to liken their appearance to rebellious figures such as Marlon Brando and James Dean, suggesting they looked like "punks." "There was the count five, the barbarians, the standels, the trogs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Mid-60s Garage Band
xref.body: The Troggs were listed as one of the rough, ragged, and raw-sounding bands from the 1960s, emerging from North American garages and basements. Their rebellious aesthetic, often featuring leather jackets, drew comparisons to figures like Marlon Brando and James Dean, leading some to describe them visually as "punks." "There was the count five, the barbarians, the standels, the trogs."
